title: Vedanta Aluminium Seeks $1.4 Billion Bank Loan in First Major Move After Demerger
excerpt: The newly independent aluminium unit is raising ₹13,500 crore from banks as Vedanta's post-split entities begin charting separate financial paths, while the parent refinances $5.2 billion in dollar debt.
body:
• Vedanta Aluminium Metal, newly listed after the five-way demerger of Vedanta Ltd, is seeking a ₹13,500 crore ($1.4 billion) bank loan — the first major financing by any of the demerged entities
  • At the parent level, Vedanta Resources is refinancing $5.2 billion in dollar bonds and loans, targeting a 300-basis-point reduction in borrowing costs after securing credit rating upgrades from S&P and Moody's
  • The demerger split Vedanta Ltd into five independently listed companies: Vedanta Aluminium, Vedanta Oil & Gas, Vedanta Power, Vedanta Iron & Steel, and the residual Vedanta Ltd anchored by its Hindustan Zinc stake
  • Net debt at the parent level has fallen to $4.9 billion from $8.9 billion five years ago, driven by aggressive deleveraging and dividend upstream from subsidiaries

Vedanta Aluminium Metal Ltd is seeking a ₹13,500 crore ($1.4 billion) bank loan, marking the first major financing move by any of the entities created in billionaire Anil Agarwal's landmark demerger of Vedanta Ltd earlier this year.

The loan signals that India's largest aluminium producer is wasting no time establishing an independent financial identity after separating from the Vedanta conglomerate in a five-way split completed in April — one of the biggest corporate restructurings in Indian metals and mining history.

The Demerger Landscape

Vedanta Ltd was split into five separately listed companies under a 1:1 scheme: shareholders received one share each of Vedanta Aluminium Metal, Vedanta Oil & Gas, Vedanta Power, and Vedanta Iron & Steel for every share held. The residual Vedanta Ltd retains its stake in Hindustan Zinc and other base-metal assets.

The stock turned ex-demerger on April 30, with shares adjusting from ₹773.6 to ₹289.5 in a special pre-open session. Early trading was mixed — Iron & Steel surged while Aluminium and Oil & Gas hit lower circuits — but the aggregate market value of the demerged entities exceeded the pre-split conglomerate valuation, validating the value-unlocking thesis.

Parent-Level Refinancing

While the aluminium unit raises fresh rupee debt, parent company Vedanta Resources Ltd is executing a $5.2 billion refinancing of its dollar bonds and loans. The UK-based conglomerate has hired Barclays, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, and JPMorgan for the deal, which aims to replace expensive debt and lower average borrowing costs from about 10%.

"The deal is likely to smooth the company's debt maturity profile and cut medium-term repayment and refinance risks."

— Mary Ellen Olson, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst

A separate unit recently accepted bids worth $1.75 billion for a three-tranche dollar bond issuance, further demonstrating improved market access. Both S&P Global and Moody's upgraded Vedanta Resources' credit ratings last month, reflecting the deleveraging progress — net debt has dropped to $4.9 billion from $8.9 billion over five years.

Investment Implications

For investors with exposure to Indian metals, the demerger offers targeted sector bets rather than a conglomerate discount. Analysts note that the aluminium and power businesses are capital-intensive and relatively debt-heavy, with limited near-term dividend flexibility. The oil & gas unit, largely debt-free, may be better positioned for cash distributions but remains sensitive to crude prices.

The Agarwal family's need to upstream cash from subsidiaries to service debt at the parent level — a longstanding structural feature of the Vedanta group — is expected to continue across all demerged entities.

What's Next

The aluminium loan will fund capacity expansion at a time when global demand for the metal is rising, driven by electric vehicles, renewable energy, and construction. The success of this first post-demerger financing will set the template for how the other Vedanta entities approach capital markets independently, and test whether lenders are comfortable with the new, simpler corporate structure.
